title: Habits to unlearn
goal: Replace common Indian-English phrases with international ones
intro: Indian English is a real variety of English, and many of its phrases are fine at home. But some of them confuse people from other countries or sound old-fashioned. Knowing the international version lets you choose: “prepone”, “passed out”, “cousin brother”, “out of station”, “do the needful” and “What is your good name?”.

examples: Can we bring the meeting forward to 10?

rules.rule: passed out (of college) → graduated. (“Passed out” means fainted!)
cousin brother / sister → cousin. out of station → out of town / away.
examples: I’m out of town this week.

rules.rule: What is your good name? → May I know your name? / What’s your name?
examples: Could I have your name, please?

mistakes.right: Can we move the call earlier?

mistakes.wrong: I passed out from college in 2019.
I am out of station till Monday.
mistakes.right: I’m out of town until Monday.
Please could you process this? (say the exact action)

ex.q: Can we ___ the meeting to 9 am?
My ___ is getting married next month.
I’ll be ___ next week, visiting my parents.
My cousin sister lives in Canada.
We need to prepone the launch.
ex.fixed: We need to bring forward the launch.

ex.q: I passed out from engineering college last year.
ex.fixed: I graduated from engineering college last year.

ex.q: I’m out of ___ for two days, so call me on my mobile.

ex.a: Could we move the meeting to an earlier time?

ex.q: Say it the international way: “I passed out in 2015.”

talk: Introduce your education and family, and explain a change in your schedule, without using prepone, passed out, cousin brother or out of station.
